items.stem: The “free silver” campaign of 1896 received its greatest popular support from
items.stimulus: “We have witnessed for more than a quarter of a century the struggles of the two great political parties for power and plunder, while grievous wrongs have been inflicted upon the suffering people. We charge that the controlling influences dominating both these parties have permitted the existing dreadful conditions to develop without serious effort to prevent or restrain them. Neither do they now promise us any substantial reform. They have agreed together to ignore, in the coming campaign, every issue but one. They propose to drown the outcries of a plundered people with the uproar of a sham battle over the tariff, so that capitalists, corporations, national banks, rings, trusts, watered stock, the demonetization of silver and the oppressions of the usurers may all be lost sight of. They propose to sacrifice our homes, lives, and children on the altar of mammon; to destroy the multitude in order to secure corruption funds from the millionaires. “Assembled on the anniversary of the birthday of the nation, and filled with the spirit of the grand general and chief who established our independence, we seek to restore the government of the Republic to the hands of ‘the plain people,’ with which class it originated. We assert our purposes to be identical with the purposes of the National Constitution; to form a more perfect union and establish justice, insure domestic tranquility, provide for the common defence, promote the general welfare, and secure the blessings of liberty for ourselves and our posterity.” Source: Populist Party Platform, 1892
options: New England businessmen, who were discriminated against under the existing banking system
southern women, who incorporated it into a larger campaign for economic equality
bankers, who had run out of paper currency to invest
farmers, who hoped that a more generous money supply would ease their debt burdens
items.explanation: The “free silver” campaign aimed to increase the money supply through the free coinage of silver. It was the great cause of the Populist Party, which argued that the existing monetary practices favored the wealthy and elite, particularly in the Northeast. Free coinage of silver, the party argued, would cause inflation but would also put more money in circulation, making it easier for farmers to pay off their debts. Furthermore, Populists felt that a larger money supply was appropriate to the United States’ tremendous growth rate at that time. The policy was naturally quite popular with farmers, but not with bankers, who would have had their loans repaid with devalued currency. Free silver was a central issue in the 1896 election, during which the Populists and the Democratic Party joined forces.

option_explanations.A: New England businessmen favored the gold standard and tight money; they opposed free silver, which threatened creditor interests.
option_explanations.B: Southern women were not the constituency of the free-silver campaign. It was an agrarian movement led by male Populists and westerners.
option_explanations.C: Bankers favored the gold standard and opposed free silver — inflation would erode the value of the loans they held.
option_explanations.D: Farmers carried heavy debts fixed in dollars while crop prices fell. Free coinage of silver would expand the money supply and create inflation, making debts easier to repay — the heart of the Populist 'free silver' crusade of 1896.

items.stem: All of the following from 1870 to 1900 could be used to support the claims advanced by the authors in the party platform EXCEPT
items.stimulus: “We have witnessed for more than a quarter of a century the struggles of the two great political parties for power and plunder, while grievous wrongs have been inflicted upon the suffering people. We charge that the controlling influences dominating both these parties have permitted the existing dreadful conditions to develop without serious effort to prevent or restrain them. Neither do they now promise us any substantial reform. They have agreed together to ignore, in the coming campaign, every issue but one. They propose to drown the outcries of a plundered people with the uproar of a sham battle over the tariff, so that capitalists, corporations, national banks, rings, trusts, watered stock, the demonetization of silver and the oppressions of the usurers may all be lost sight of. They propose to sacrifice our homes, lives, and children on the altar of mammon; to destroy the multitude in order to secure corruption funds from the millionaires. “Assembled on the anniversary of the birthday of the nation, and filled with the spirit of the grand general and chief who established our independence, we seek to restore the government of the Republic to the hands of ‘the plain people,’ with which class it originated. We assert our purposes to be identical with the purposes of the National Constitution; to form a more perfect union and establish justice, insure domestic tranquility, provide for the common defence, promote the general welfare, and secure the blessings of liberty for ourselves and our posterity.” Source: Populist Party Platform, 1892
options: the creation of civil service laws like the Pendleton Act
courts’ interpretations of the Sherman Antitrust Act
the existence of urban political machines like Tammany Hall
railroad scandals like Credit Mobilier
items.explanation: The authors here are arguing that both Republicans and Democrats in the Gilded Age have no interest in supporting the common man and are mostly corrupt, so you need an example that shows that not being the case. Even though the Sherman Act might seem to be designed to bring corporations to heel, courts did not interpret it that way when this was written, so eliminate (B). Tammany Hall mostly operated off graft, eliminating (C). Credit Mobilier also shows politicians being bought off by corporate interests, so eliminate (D). Choose (A) because the Pendleton Act sought to professionalize the Civil Service and keep politicians from using government jobs for patronage.

option_explanations.A: The Pendleton Act (1883) replaced patronage hiring with merit-based civil service — a genuine reform serving the public interest. It contradicts the platform's claim that both parties were wholly corrupt, so it is the exception.
option_explanations.B: Courts interpreted the Sherman Antitrust Act narrowly and even turned it against labor unions, leaving corporate power untouched — supporting the platform's corruption claim, not the exception.
option_explanations.C: Tammany Hall ran on graft and patronage — supporting the platform's corruption claim, not the exception.
option_explanations.D: The Credit Mobilier scandal showed congressmen bought off with railroad stock — supporting the platform's corruption claim, not the exception.

items.stem: Which of the following is LEAST associated with the Populist movement?
items.stimulus: “We have witnessed for more than a quarter of a century the struggles of the two great political parties for power and plunder, while grievous wrongs have been inflicted upon the suffering people. We charge that the controlling influences dominating both these parties have permitted the existing dreadful conditions to develop without serious effort to prevent or restrain them. Neither do they now promise us any substantial reform. They have agreed together to ignore, in the coming campaign, every issue but one. They propose to drown the outcries of a plundered people with the uproar of a sham battle over the tariff, so that capitalists, corporations, national banks, rings, trusts, watered stock, the demonetization of silver and the oppressions of the usurers may all be lost sight of. They propose to sacrifice our homes, lives, and children on the altar of mammon; to destroy the multitude in order to secure corruption funds from the millionaires. “Assembled on the anniversary of the birthday of the nation, and filled with the spirit of the grand general and chief who established our independence, we seek to restore the government of the Republic to the hands of ‘the plain people,’ with which class it originated. We assert our purposes to be identical with the purposes of the National Constitution; to form a more perfect union and establish justice, insure domestic tranquility, provide for the common defence, promote the general welfare, and secure the blessings of liberty for ourselves and our posterity.” Source: Populist Party Platform, 1892
options: Support of labor unions
Secret ballot elections
Free coinage of silver
Ending regulation of railroads
items.explanation: Western Populists resented the control that the railroads exerted over transportation of goods across the country and wished to see railroads more tightly controlled by the federal government. All other answers represent Populist causes.

option_explanations.A: Populists supported labor unions and the eight-hour day — associated with the movement, not the exception.
option_explanations.B: The secret (Australian) ballot was a Populist demand to curb intimidation at the polls — associated, not the exception.
option_explanations.C: Free coinage of silver was the Populists' signature monetary demand — associated, not the exception.
option_explanations.D: Populists wanted more railroad regulation, not less — many demanded government ownership of the railroads. Ending regulation is the opposite of their position, so it is least associated.

items.stem: Which of the following was most directly a cause of the success of the Populist Party?
items.stimulus: “We have witnessed for more than a quarter of a century the struggles of the two great political parties for power and plunder, while grievous wrongs have been inflicted upon the suffering people. We charge that the controlling influences dominating both these parties have permitted the existing dreadful conditions to develop without serious effort to prevent or restrain them. Neither do they now promise us any substantial reform. They have agreed together to ignore, in the coming campaign, every issue but one. They propose to drown the outcries of a plundered people with the uproar of a sham battle over the tariff, so that capitalists, corporations, national banks, rings, trusts, watered stock, the demonetization of silver and the oppressions of the usurers may all be lost sight of. They propose to sacrifice our homes, lives, and children on the altar of mammon; to destroy the multitude in order to secure corruption funds from the millionaires. “Assembled on the anniversary of the birthday of the nation, and filled with the spirit of the grand general and chief who established our independence, we seek to restore the government of the Republic to the hands of ‘the plain people,’ with which class it originated. We assert our purposes to be identical with the purposes of the National Constitution; to form a more perfect union and establish justice, insure domestic tranquility, provide for the common defence, promote the general welfare, and secure the blessings of liberty for ourselves and our posterity.” Source: Populist Party Platform, 1892
options: Western farmers and ranchers favored conservation and organized to promote the National Parks system.
The growth of corporate power and banking interests inspired rural activists to lobby for political reform.
Western farmers resisted the mechanization of agriculture and resented government interference in rural affairs.
After the Civil War, westward migration slowed, causing a long-term recession in many Western territories.
items.explanation: The Populists generally resented big business and banking interests and saw their power as working contrary to the interests of farmers, ranchers, and working people in general. Most Populists lived in rural areas, although later Populists championed the causes of urban factory workers. Conservation was not a prominent concern for Populists, so rule out (A). Western farmers did not resent government interference; in fact, they often welcomed it, so rule out (C). Westward migration did not slow after the Civil War; it increased, so rule out (D).

option_explanations.A: Conservation and the National Parks system were not Populist causes; they belonged to the later Roosevelt-era conservation movement.
option_explanations.B: The Populist Party grew directly out of rural anger at corporate and banking power — railroads, trusts, and banks squeezing farmers — which drove farmers and ranchers to organize for political reform.
option_explanations.C: Western farmers did not resist mechanization or resent government interference; they demanded government action (regulation, silver coinage) on their behalf.
option_explanations.D: Westward migration accelerated, not slowed, after the Civil War. There was no migration-driven western recession.

items.stem: Which of the following conclusions is best supported by the excerpt above?
options: Lincoln won the populous Northern states; McClellan carried sparser ones.
Lincoln won the Election of 1864 because of Union successes during the Civil War.
The Emancipation Proclamation mobilized Black voters in the South to vote for Lincoln in the Election of 1864.
Republicans managed to gain control of Congress through the efforts of Lincoln to campaign on their behalf.
items.explanation: This question is all about Process of Elimination (POE). There is no mention of Black voters, so rule out (C). Choice (D) is tempting, but you don’t know for sure if Lincoln was campaigning for any other Republicans. Choice (B) is likewise unsupported. Choice (A) must be true because Lincoln won so many Electoral College votes. New Jersey and Delaware are relatively small states, while Kentucky was rural in 1864.

option_explanations.A: Lincoln's 212-to-21 Electoral College landslide, with McClellan carrying only New Jersey, Delaware, and Kentucky, means Lincoln swept the populous Northern states while McClellan held a few smaller, sparser ones.
option_explanations.B: The excerpt describes who voted and who won, not why. It offers no evidence connecting Union military successes to Lincoln's victory.
option_explanations.C: The excerpt never mentions Black voters. Black men could not vote in most states in 1864 — the 15th Amendment came in 1870.
option_explanations.D: The excerpt says Republicans widened their congressional majorities but does not show Lincoln campaigning on other Republicans' behalf.

items.stimulus: Paraphrased excerpt (facts and statistics only; not a quotation) — “1864: Lincoln v. McClellan,” Harpweek.com: About 78 percent of the Union electorate cast ballots in 1864. Lincoln won reelection in an Electoral College landslide, 212 votes to McClellan’s 21, and took about 55 percent of the popular vote — the third-largest share of the nineteenth century. McClellan carried only New Jersey, Delaware, and Kentucky. Lincoln’s coalition drew heavily on native-born farmers, skilled and professional workers, voters of New England descent, younger voters, and military personnel (he won an estimated 78 percent of the Union soldier and sailor vote); Democrats ran strongest in the cities and among Irish- and German-American voters. Republicans also widened their congressional majorities (149 to 42 in the House, 42 to 10 in the Senate), retook several state legislatures, and lost only the New Jersey governorship.

items.stem: Which of the following provides the best explanation for why Radical Republicans opposed Lincoln in 1861?
options: Lincoln’s decision to issue the Emancipation Proclamation was done without congressional oversight.
The Radical Republicans wanted immediate emancipation of enslaved people, but Lincoln refused to cooperate.
Lincoln’s Ten Percent Plan provided no assurance of Black suffrage.
Lincoln’s appointment of Andrew Johnson as vice president clashed with the Reconstruction goals of the Senate.
items.explanation: When the Union dissolved and the South left Congress, Lincoln was faced with a legislature much more progressive in its thoughts on slavery than he was. The Radical Republican wing of Congress wanted immediate emancipation. Choices (A), (C), and (D) are all post-1861.

option_explanations.A: The Emancipation Proclamation was issued in 1863. It cannot explain Radical opposition to Lincoln in 1861.
option_explanations.B: In 1861 the Radical Republican wing demanded immediate emancipation, while Lincoln refused — insisting his priority was preserving the Union, not ending slavery. That refusal is what set them against him.
option_explanations.C: The Ten Percent Plan was announced in December 1863, not 1861.
option_explanations.D: Andrew Johnson was not nominated for vice president until 1864, not 1861.

items.stem: Of the following policies, which was NOT a main objective of American Progressives?
options: Passage of the Pure Food and Water Act
Creation of national forests and protected wildlife reserves
Initiation of antitrust lawsuits against various corporate monopolies
Intervention in the affairs of Central American governments
items.explanation: The Progressives pursued no coherent foreign policy, per se. Although Theodore Roosevelt was interested in Central American affairs, he was not representing primarily Progressive ideals with this initiative.

option_explanations.A: The Progressive-era pure-food law (1906) was a classic Progressive objective — consumer protection through federal regulation, not the exception.
option_explanations.B: Creating national forests and wildlife reserves was Theodore Roosevelt's conservation crusade — a core Progressive objective, not the exception.
option_explanations.C: Antitrust lawsuits against corporate monopolies were a core Progressive objective — not the exception.
option_explanations.D: Intervening in Central American governments (Panama, the Roosevelt Corollary) was Roosevelt's imperialism, not a Progressive domestic-reform objective — this is the exception.

items.stem: The ideas expressed in the passage would be most supported by which of the following groups?
options: Industrial railroad owners
Immigrant factory workers
Urban middle-class professionals
Rural tenant farmers
items.explanation: This question wants you to figure out which group in the country found Progressive ideas most appealing. You can eliminate (A) because “industrial justice” probably would have been a red flag for them. You can eliminate (D) because Progressive policy had its biggest purchase in cities in the 1900s, so the appeal to a tenant farmer would have been minimal. For (B), “immigrant factory workers” might be tempting, but it’s important to know that Progressives tended to be far wealthier than the people they were claiming to help (many of whom found those Progressives quite patronizing), so the best answer would be (C).

option_explanations.A: Industrial railroad owners would have been alarmed by talk of 'industrial justice' and government regulation — not the Progressive base.
option_explanations.B: Progressives were far wealthier than immigrant factory workers. Workers might sympathize, but they were not the movement's core constituency.
option_explanations.C: Progressivism was largely an urban middle-class movement — professionals like lawyers, doctors, journalists, and ministers who sought rational, expert-led reform of city and industrial life.
option_explanations.D: Rural tenant farmers were the Populists' base of the 1890s. Progressive policy had its greatest purchase in the cities, so tenant farmers were not its core supporters.

items.stimulus: “The conscience of the people, in a time of grave national problems, has called into being a new party, born of the nation’s sense of justice. We of the Progressive party here dedicate ourselves to the fulfillment of the duty laid upon us by our fathers to maintain the government of the people, by the people and for the people whose foundations they laid. We hold with Thomas Jefferson and Abraham Lincoln that the people are the masters of their Constitution, to fulfill its purposes and to safeguard it from those who, by perversion of its intent, would convert it into an instrument of injustice. In accordance with the needs of each generation the people must use their sovereign powers to establish and maintain equal opportunity and industrial justice, to secure which this Government was founded and without which no republic can endure. “This country belongs to the people who inhabit it. Its resources, its business, its institutions and its laws should be utilized, maintained or altered in whatever manner will best promote the general interest. It is time to set the public welfare in the first place.” Source: Progressive Party Platform, 1912 (public domain).

items.stem: Which of the following policies would be the biggest source of disagreement between the Progressive platform above and Populists of the 1890s?
options: Laws designed to break up monopolies
Laws allowing for direct election of senators
Laws designed to create a progressive income tax
Laws designed to nationalize the American rail system
items.explanation: Populists and Progressives certainly had a lot of areas where they agreed, but it’s important to remember that they weren’t identical, and there were some areas where they differed greatly. Progressives like Teddy Roosevelt did help break up monopolies, and they were broadly supportive of efforts to tax income and directly elect senators. However, Progressives still tended to be middle-class liberals, meaning that they were skeptical of a government that was too heavy-handed. Whereas Populists would prefer the government taking over the rail system, Progressives preferred things like regulating them with the FTC. For that reason, (D) is the best answer here.

option_explanations.A: Both movements favored breaking up monopolies — an area of agreement, not disagreement.
option_explanations.B: Both supported the direct election of senators (achieved in the 17th Amendment, 1913) — an area of agreement, not disagreement.
option_explanations.C: Both supported a progressive income tax (achieved in the 16th Amendment, 1913) — an area of agreement, not disagreement.
option_explanations.D: Populists demanded government ownership of the railroads. Middle-class Progressives, skeptical of heavy-handed state control of industry, would not go that far — the biggest source of disagreement.

items.stem: In harmony with the sentiments of the excerpt above, which of the following best characterizes the Square Deal of Theodore Roosevelt?
options: Conservation, trust-busting, consumer protection
Protective tariffs, centralized banking, conservation
Equal opportunity, women’s suffrage, laissez-faire economics
Laissez-faire economics, support of labor unions, conservation
items.explanation: Theodore Roosevelt’s Square Deal program was designed to conserve Earth’s resources, control corporations through government regulation, and protect the consumer.

option_explanations.A: The Square Deal's three aims were conservation of natural resources, control of corporations (trust-busting and regulation), and consumer protection — the 'three C's' of Roosevelt's domestic program.
option_explanations.B: Protective tariffs and centralized banking were not the Square Deal's defining features; its core was conservation, corporate regulation, and consumer protection.
option_explanations.C: Laissez-faire economics contradicts the Square Deal entirely — Roosevelt expanded federal regulation, the opposite of leaving business alone.
option_explanations.D: Laissez-faire economics contradicts the Square Deal. Labor support and conservation alone, without corporate regulation, do not capture it.

items.stem: Progressivism was challenged by all of the following in the 1920s EXCEPT
options: a desire to “return to normalcy” after the First World War
an influx of more conservative immigrants skeptical of Progressivism’s goals
a fear of government overreach in the wake of the Russian Revolution
a backlash against higher taxes by wealthy business owners
items.explanation: The 1920s saw the decline of Progressivism, and most of these help explain why. Warren Harding campaigned on a “return to Normalcy” that saw the United States become more isolationist, challenging Progressive imperialism, so eliminate (A). Some sympathetic to Progressivism were explicitly socialist (like Robert LaFollette), which became an easy scapegoat against the movement, eliminating (C). Treasury Secretary Andrew Mellon was known for cutting taxes for wealthy Americans in the wake of Progressivism, so remove (D). However, the 1920s saw huge cuts to immigration, not an influx, so (B) is the best answer.

option_explanations.A: Harding's 'return to normalcy' — turning away from wartime progressivism and reform — genuinely challenged Progressivism, so it is not the exception.
option_explanations.B: Immigration was sharply restricted in the 1920s (the 1921 and 1924 quota acts), and there was no influx of conservative immigrants undermining Progressivism. The movement's challengers were native-born: normalcy advocates, Red Scare anti-radicals, and tax-cutting businessmen — so this is the exception.
option_explanations.C: Fear of government overreach and radicalism after the Russian Revolution (the Red Scare) genuinely challenged Progressivism, so it is not the exception.
option_explanations.D: The backlash against high wartime taxes — Mellon's tax cuts for the wealthy — genuinely challenged the Progressive regulatory state, so it is not the exception.

items.stem: The 1933 political cartoon shown above makes the point that
options: infighting within and among unions prevented their rise to economic power
government inspectors turned their backs to illegal repression of labor unions
attacks on unions were so well-concealed that the government did not know where to begin its investigations
from their beginnings, labor unions were controlled by organized crime
items.explanation: The cartoon depicts the government conducting a misdirected fact-finding mission at a time when abuses against labor unions were obvious. The attack is not “well-concealed,” so rule out (C).

option_explanations.A: The cartoon shows no union infighting. It shows outside thugs beating a worker while the government investigator looks away.
option_explanations.B: The two thugs labeled 'STRIKE-BREAKING' and 'UNION-BUSTING' beat a helpless worker with clubs while the small 'FACT-FINDING' figure — the government investigator — crawls on all fours with a magnifying glass, deliberately looking away. The point is that the government turned its back on the violent repression of unions.
option_explanations.C: The attacks are not concealed at all — they happen in the open. The investigator sees the violence and chooses to look away, which is precisely the cartoon's charge.
option_explanations.D: The cartoon does not claim unions were mob-controlled. The worker is the victim here, not a gangster.

items.stimulus: [Described image — 1933 political cartoon titled ‘Strike-Breaking’ (original artwork not reproduced). Two burly thugs, one labeled ‘STRIKE-BREAKING’ and the other ‘UNION-BUSTING,’ beat a helpless worker with clubs. In the foreground, a small figure labeled ‘FACT-FINDING’ — a government investigator — crawls on all fours holding a magnifying glass, deliberately looking away from the violence. The cartoon charges that employers violently repressed unions while the federal government offered only a willfully blind, ineffectual ‘fact-finding’ response.]

items.stem: Which of the following acts was the most beneficial to the labor movement?
options: The Clayton Antitrust Act, which legalized strikes and picketing
The Sherman Antitrust Act, which prevented corporations from monopolizing markets
The Elkins Act, which provided greater regulation of railroads
The Hepburn Act, which regulated public modes of transportation
items.explanation: Samuel Gompers once referred to the Clayton Antitrust Act as “The Magna Carta of Labor,” because in addition to strengthening the Sherman Antitrust Act, it also exempted labor unions from antitrust prosecution and legalized strikes and picketing.

option_explanations.A: The Clayton Antitrust Act (1914) exempted labor unions from antitrust prosecution and explicitly legalized strikes and picketing — which is why Samuel Gompers called it the 'Magna Carta of Labor.'
option_explanations.B: The Sherman Antitrust Act (1890) was aimed at corporate monopolies but was used more often against unions (as in the Danbury Hatters case) than for them.
option_explanations.C: The Elkins Act (1903) targeted railroad rebates — a transportation regulation, not a labor-rights measure.
option_explanations.D: The Hepburn Act (1906) strengthened ICC regulation of railroads — a transportation measure, not a labor-rights measure.

items.stem: Which of the following statements about organized labor in the early 1900s is true?
options: Throughout the early 1900s, Congress promoted the interests of labor unions over captains of industry.
Immigrants helped to promote a more diverse workforce less reliant on child labor.
Sharecroppers in the South largely voted for Democrats who championed labor causes.
unions such as the American Federation of Labor bargained directly with employers for workplace changes
items.explanation: Congress did not consistently promote the interests of labor unions, so rule out (A). Republicans, in particular, tended to try to curb the power of labor. Immigrants were not a large part of labor union membership, nor did they displace child workers (laws banning child labor accomplished this), so rule out (B). Black sharecroppers may have voted for Democrats, but they did not have a direct influence, so rule out (C). Thus, the success of labor unions was largely due to their own efforts.

option_explanations.A: Congress did not consistently promote unions; Republicans in particular repeatedly tried to curb labor's power (e.g., court injunctions against strikes).
option_explanations.B: Immigrants were not a large share of early union membership, and child labor declined because of child-labor laws, not because immigrants displaced child workers.
option_explanations.C: Black sharecroppers in the South had almost no political influence in the early 1900s; this option is garbled history.
option_explanations.D: The American Federation of Labor's craft unions won workplace gains primarily through their own efforts — bargaining directly with employers for wages, hours, and conditions.

items.stem: A historian could use this political cartoon to prove which of the following claims?
options: Supporters of organized labor were critical of government policies around unions.
Companies often violently attacked workers who tried to unionize.
Workers at unionized shops tended to enjoy better working conditions than those at non-unionized shops.
Capitalists were unfairly maligned by radical labor unions.
items.explanation: Think about how you could use this source to prove a historical claim. For (B), even though this could be true, the source here is a cartoon, meaning it’s likely an embellishment and not referring to a specific instance of this happening. For (C), this is a true statement, but nothing in the cartoon itself proves this claim. For (D), this is really more of an opinion and definitely not one the creator of the cartoon would support. However, (A) seems to accurately describe the situation in the cartoon and is provable from this, so (A) is the best answer.

option_explanations.A: The cartoon is itself a labor supporter's attack on government policy — it accuses Washington of willful blindness toward employer violence. A historian can use it to prove that labor supporters criticized government union policies.
option_explanations.B: A cartoon is an embellishment, not evidence of a specific event. It cannot prove that companies actually carried out such attacks, only that critics charged they did.
option_explanations.C: Nothing in the cartoon compares working conditions at unionized versus non-unionized shops, so it cannot prove that claim.
option_explanations.D: The cartoonist's view is the opposite: the capitalists' thugs are the villains. The cartoon does not support the claim that capitalists were unfairly maligned.

In the foreground, a small figure labeled ‘FACT-FINDING’ — a government investigator — crawls on all fours holding a magnifying glass, deliberately looking away from the violence. The cartoon charges that employers violently repressed unions while the federal government offered only a willfully blind, ineffectual ‘fact-finding’ response.]

items.stem: How was the Red Scare in post–World War I America connected to organized labor movements?
options: Unrestricted immigration after World War I flooded the job markets with low-wage workers, leading to resentment by union members and accusations of communist sympathies.
California migrant workers were largely Italian immigrants, many of whom had anarchist leanings.
Labor unions were largely thought to be controlled by liberals with Marxist sympathies.
Senator Joseph McCarthy, a Wisconsin Republican, was hostile to both communism and labor unions, fueling suspicion among American Conservatives.
items.explanation: Although it was by no means universal, many early 20th-century union leaders were, in fact, Communists or sympathetic to socialist ideologies. (This tendency reversed after World War II.) Choice (A) may have some kernel of truth, but it is not the primary cause of the anti-labor sentiment. Choice (D) is incorrect because McCarthy was most vocal in the 1950s.

option_explanations.A: Immigration was restricted, not unrestricted, after World War I (the 1921 Emergency Quota Act). This was not the primary link between the Red Scare and labor.
option_explanations.B: California migrant farmworkers were not largely Italian anarchists. This misdescribes both the workforce and the connection.
option_explanations.C: Many early-20th-century union leaders were Communists or sympathetic to socialist ideas (a tendency that reversed after World War II), so unions were widely suspected of Marxist sympathies — the real link between the postwar Red Scare and organized labor.
option_explanations.D: Senator Joseph McCarthy belongs to the 1950s Second Red Scare, not the post-World War I Red Scare of 1919-20.

items.stem: The Supreme Court decision above is best understood in the context of
items.stimulus: “We conclude that, in the field of public education, the doctrine of ‘separate but equal’ has no place. Separate educational facilities are inherently unequal. Therefore, we hold that the plaintiffs and others similarly situated for whom the actions have been brought are, by reason of the segregation complained of, deprived of the equal protection of the laws guaranteed by the Fourteenth Amendment.” Source: Brown v. Board of Education , 1954
options: a resurgence of social conservatism in the wake of World War II
an invigorated postwar economy as countries rebuilt after the war
activists' postwar push for civil liberties at home after defeating tyranny abroad
a fear of communist government subversion in the wake of Stalinist expansion
items.explanation: While all of these statements describe things that were happening in the 1950s, only one of them is relevant to the stimulus at hand. The court case here is famous for outlawing segregation in public schools. While there was a good bit of social conservatism in the 1950s, this is definitely not an example of that, so eliminate (A). Even though America’s economy was booming, that’s not directly related to the issue at hand here, eliminating (B). For (D), civil rights activists were often tarred as communists, but that doesn’t explain why the Supreme Court decided in their favor here. However, (C) accurately describes the “Double V” campaign of freedom abroad and at home, so that is the best context.

option_explanations.A: Brown v. Board was a liberal expansion of rights, not an expression of social conservatism.
option_explanations.B: The postwar economic boom is real history but has no direct bearing on a school-desegregation ruling.
option_explanations.C: After defeating tyranny abroad in World War II, activists pressed the contradiction of segregation at home — the postwar civil-liberties push that produced Brown's holding that segregated schools are 'inherently unequal.'
option_explanations.D: Fear of communist subversion is not the context of Brown. The decision is about racial equality under the Fourteenth Amendment, not anti-communism.

items.stem: Which of the following best represents an effect of the legal decision described above?
items.stimulus: “We conclude that, in the field of public education, the doctrine of ‘separate but equal’ has no place. Separate educational facilities are inherently unequal. Therefore, we hold that the plaintiffs and others similarly situated for whom the actions have been brought are, by reason of the segregation complained of, deprived of the equal protection of the laws guaranteed by the Fourteenth Amendment.” Source: Brown v. Board of Education , 1954
options: Continuing white resistance slowed efforts at desegregation, sparking a series of social conflicts throughout the South.
The Supreme Court decision from Brown v. Board of Education led to increased enrollment in colleges and universities.
During the 1960s, increasing numbers of high school graduates rejected the notion that a college education was desirable.
In the 20th century, jobs in advanced technical and medical industries generally require postgraduate degrees.
items.explanation: Liberalism, based on a firm belief in the efficacy of governmental and especially federal power to achieve social goals at home, reached its apex in the mid-1960s and generated a variety of political and cultural responses. Southern Conservatives did not accept the goals of civil rights liberals without a struggle. Riots and protests erupted throughout the South, while Little Rock, Arkansas, refused to integrate its high school for some time. Choices (B) and (C) are unsupportable, while (D) cannot be directly attributed to Brown v. Board of Education .

option_explanations.A: Brown did not desegregate schools overnight. 'Massive resistance' across the South — Little Rock's defiance in 1957, riots and protests — slowed desegregation and sparked years of social conflict.
option_explanations.B: Brown had no direct effect on college and university enrollment levels.
option_explanations.C: There is no evidence that 1960s high school graduates broadly rejected college as undesirable.
option_explanations.D: Postgraduate requirements for technical and medical jobs are unrelated to a school-desegregation decision.

items.stem: All of the following are social movements inspired by the Supreme Court decision referenced above EXCEPT
items.stimulus: “We conclude that, in the field of public education, the doctrine of ‘separate but equal’ has no place. Separate educational facilities are inherently unequal. Therefore, we hold that the plaintiffs and others similarly situated for whom the actions have been brought are, by reason of the segregation complained of, deprived of the equal protection of the laws guaranteed by the Fourteenth Amendment.” Source: Brown v. Board of Education , 1954
options: women’s rights
gay and lesbian rights
states’ rights
Native American rights
items.explanation: Many formerly oppressed groups were inspired to take action after the successes of the civil rights movement. States’ rights, however, was never a social movement in the same manner as the others.

option_explanations.A: The women's rights movement drew directly on the civil-rights model — marches, litigation, legislation — so it was inspired by Brown's success, not the exception.
option_explanations.B: The gay and lesbian rights movement drew on the civil-rights model of equality claims, so it was inspired by the post-Brown movement, not the exception.
option_explanations.C: 'States' rights' was the segregationists' counter-doctrine used to resist Brown, not a liberation movement inspired by it — this is the exception.
option_explanations.D: The Native American rights (Red Power) movement of the late 1960s drew on the civil-rights model, so it was inspired by the post-Brown movement, not the exception.

items.stem: Desegregation of schools was, in part, a response to unfulfilled promises from which of the following initiatives?
items.stimulus: “We conclude that, in the field of public education, the doctrine of ‘separate but equal’ has no place. Separate educational facilities are inherently unequal. Therefore, we hold that the plaintiffs and others similarly situated for whom the actions have been brought are, by reason of the segregation complained of, deprived of the equal protection of the laws guaranteed by the Fourteenth Amendment.” Source: Brown v. Board of Education , 1954
options: The Great Society
The Square Deal
The New Deal
Reconstruction
items.explanation: Reconstruction had originally intended to integrate freed enslaved people into southern white society, but it largely failed to do so. Civil rights leaders picked up the banner and sought to get the equal rights they had legally earned after the Civil War.

option_explanations.A: The Great Society (1960s) came after Brown (1954), so it cannot be the unfulfilled promise Brown was answering.
option_explanations.B: The Square Deal (1900s) never promised school integration.
option_explanations.C: The New Deal (1930s) never promised school desegregation.
option_explanations.D: Reconstruction promised Black equality through the 13th, 14th, and 15th Amendments but failed to deliver it as Jim Crow took hold. The mid-20th-century civil-rights movement resumed that unfinished work, culminating in Brown.

items.stem: All of the following are factors that contributed to the prominence of conservatism in the late 1970s and 1980s EXCEPT
items.stimulus: “If you analyze it I believe the very heart and soul of conservatism is libertarianism. The basis of conservatism is a desire for less government interference or less centralized authority or more individual freedom and this is a pretty general description also of what libertarianism is. ... I believe there are legitimate government functions. There is a legitimate need in an orderly society for some government to maintain freedom or we will have tyranny by individuals.” Source: Ronald Reagan, interview in Reason magazine, 1975 (brief excerpt).
options: the success of the Libertarian Party in national elections
the growth of religious fundamentalism
perceived economic and foreign policy failures under President Carter
social changes following the civil rights movement and Vietnam War
items.explanation: Public confidence and trust in government declined in the 1970s in the wake of economic inflation, political scandals, and foreign policy crises, such as the Iranian hostage crisis, so rule out (C). The rapid and substantial growth of evangelical and fundamentalist Christian churches and organizations, as well as increased political participation by some of those groups, encouraged significant opposition to liberal social and political trends—rule out (B) and (D). Libertarians never had much success in national elections, so (A) is the exception.

option_explanations.A: The Libertarian Party never achieved significant success in national elections. It did not drive conservatism's rise — this is the exception.
option_explanations.B: The rapid growth of evangelical and fundamentalist churches and their political mobilization genuinely fueled conservatism, so this is not the exception.
option_explanations.C: Perceived failures under Carter — inflation and the Iranian hostage crisis — genuinely fueled conservatism, so this is not the exception.
option_explanations.D: The social upheavals following the civil-rights movement and Vietnam genuinely pushed many Americans toward conservatism, so this is not the exception.

items.stem: Which of the following groups would be most opposed to the sentiments expressed in the excerpt above?
items.stimulus: “If you analyze it I believe the very heart and soul of conservatism is libertarianism. The basis of conservatism is a desire for less government interference or less centralized authority or more individual freedom and this is a pretty general description also of what libertarianism is. ... I believe there are legitimate government functions. There is a legitimate need in an orderly society for some government to maintain freedom or we will have tyranny by individuals.” Source: Ronald Reagan, interview in Reason magazine, 1975 (brief excerpt).
options: Neoconservatives
Reagan Democrats
Progressive Liberals
Populists
items.explanation: Progressive Liberals would have been most opposed to Reagan’s conservative principles. Choice (B), Reagan Democrats, were more moderate in their views, while (D), Populists, were not entirely liberal in their views.

option_explanations.A: Neoconservatives largely shared Reagan's conservative principles, especially on anti-communism and limited government — not his most opposed critics.
option_explanations.B: Reagan Democrats were moderate Democrats who crossed over to support Reagan — sympathizers, not opponents.
option_explanations.C: Progressive liberals, who favor an active federal government for social and economic justice, were the most opposed to Reagan's small-government, libertarian-inflected conservatism.
option_explanations.D: The Populists were an 1890s agrarian movement — the wrong era and not the liberal opposition to Reagan.

items.stem: Which of the following programs is most related to Johnson’s claim that the Great Society is “a place where man can renew contact with nature”?
items.stimulus: “The challenge of the next half century is whether we have the wisdom to use wealth to enrich and elevate our national life, and to advance the quality of our American civilization…. The Great Society rests on abundance and liberty for all. It demands an end to poverty and racial injustice, to which we are totally committed in our time. But that is just the beginning. The Great Society is a place where every child can find knowledge to enrich his mind and to enlarge his talents. It is a place where leisure is a welcome chance to build and reflect, not a feared cause of boredom and restlessness. It is a place where the city of man serves not only the needs of the body and the demands of commerce but the desire for beauty and the hunger for community. It is a place where man can renew contact with nature. It is a place which honors creation for its own sake and for what it adds to the understanding of the race. It is a place where men are more concerned with the quality of their goals than the quantity of their goods. But most of all, the Great Society is not a safe harbor, a resting place, a final objective, a finished work. It is a challenge constantly renewed, beckoning us toward a destiny where the meaning of our lives matches the marvelous products of our labor.” Source: Lyndon Johnson, Remarks at the University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, 1964
options: Laws designed to give more funding to roads, highways, and mass transit
Laws designed to regulate the use of harmful chemical pesticides
Laws designed to give more funding to public broadcasting
Laws designed to give more funding to schools and colleges
items.explanation: The mention of renewing “contact with nature” should call to mind wildlife and the preservation of natural habitats. Choice (B) is the only answer that connects to these ideas. An act related to mass transportation would not likely renew contact with nature. Eliminate (A). The Public Broadcasting Act and Higher Education Acts also have aims that are not directly related to nature, so (C) and (D) are incorrect.

option_explanations.A: More funding for roads and highways has nothing to do with renewing contact with nature.
option_explanations.B: Regulating harmful chemical pesticides protects wildlife and natural habitats — the direct link to 'renewing contact with nature' (the concern Rachel Carson's Silent Spring, 1962, had made famous).
option_explanations.C: Public broadcasting funding is about media and education, not nature.
option_explanations.D: School and college funding is about education, not nature.

But most of all, the Great Society is not a safe harbor, a resting place, a final objective, a finished work. It is a challenge constantly renewed, beckoning us toward a destiny where the meaning of our lives matches the marvelous products of our labor.” Source: Lyndon Johnson, Remarks at the University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, 1964
options: the Civil Rights Act of 1964
Medicare and Medicaid
the establishment of the Department of Housing and Urban Development
the balanced budget mandate
items.explanation: All choices, except (D), were indeed part of the Great Society program. Rather than balancing the budget, the Great Society reforms meant a significant increase in federal spending, which grew faster than government revenues through taxes.

option_explanations.A: The Civil Rights Act of 1964 was a Great Society landmark — not the exception.
option_explanations.B: Medicare and Medicaid (1965) were Great Society landmarks — not the exception.
option_explanations.C: The Department of Housing and Urban Development (1965) was a Great Society creation — not the exception.
option_explanations.D: The Great Society meant a large increase in federal spending, which outran tax revenues. A balanced-budget mandate is the opposite of what the program entailed — this is the exception.

It is a challenge constantly renewed, beckoning us toward a destiny where the meaning of our lives matches the marvelous products of our labor.” Source: Lyndon Johnson, Remarks at the University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, 1964
options: undermining communism in Cuba with the Bay of Pigs Invasion
undermining communism in Vietnam after the Tet Offensive
undermining communism in Turkey and Greece using economic aid
undermining communism in the Eastern Bloc by demanding a removal of the Berlin Wall
items.explanation: Under the Lyndon B. Johnson Administration, U.S. involvement in Vietnam accelerated. Choice (A) is associated with Kennedy. Choice (C) is associated with Truman and Eisenhower. Choice (D) occurred in the late 1980s and early 1990s under Reagan and George H. W. Bush.

option_explanations.A: The Bay of Pigs invasion (1961) was Kennedy's operation, not Johnson's.
option_explanations.B: Johnson massively escalated American involvement in Vietnam (from the Gulf of Tonkin onward, through the Tet Offensive period). His Great Society rested on Cold War liberalism: fighting communism in Vietnam while building reform at home.
option_explanations.C: Economic aid to Turkey and Greece was the Truman Doctrine (1947), under Truman and Eisenhower — not Johnson.
option_explanations.D: Demanding the Berlin Wall's removal belongs to the late 1980s under Reagan and George H. W. Bush — not Johnson.

options: The New Deal
The Square Deal
The Truman Doctrine
The Monroe Doctrine
items.explanation: Today’s social welfare system stems from the New Deal; those who feel that the current American system has failed can point to Roosevelt as the man who started it all.

option_explanations.A: The Great Society was the second great wave of federal social-welfare programs, directly extending the New Deal's legacy of using federal power against poverty and insecurity.
option_explanations.B: The Square Deal was Theodore Roosevelt's Progressive-era program — the wrong predecessor for a 1960s welfare-state expansion.
option_explanations.C: The Truman Doctrine was a foreign-policy commitment to contain communism, not a domestic welfare initiative.
option_explanations.D: The Monroe Doctrine (1823) was a foreign-policy statement about the Western Hemisphere, not a domestic welfare initiative.

options: Liberal Democrats abandoned antiwar protests in a show of support for President Johnson.
Conservative Republicans mobilized to defend traditional mores and curb government authority.
Economic recession was catalyzed by increased government spending, causing “stagflation.”
A majority of Northern Black voters abandoned the Democratic Party, siding with Republicans.
items.explanation: Liberal ideals were realized in Supreme Court decisions that expanded democracy and individual freedoms, Great Society social programs and policies, and the power of the federal government, yet these unintentionally helped energize a new conservative movement that mobilized to defend traditional visions of morality and the proper role of state authority.

option_explanations.A: Liberal Democrats did not abandon antiwar protest for Johnson — the protests continued and tore the party apart in 1968.
option_explanations.B: The liberal triumphs of the 1960s — civil-rights laws, Great Society programs, Warren Court rulings — energized a conservative movement that mobilized to defend traditional morality and curb federal power.
option_explanations.C: The stagflation of the 1970s was driven by oil shocks, not directly catalyzed by 1960s government spending.
option_explanations.D: Northern Black voters remained overwhelmingly Democratic after the 1960s; they did not defect to the Republicans.
